newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS-Currencies strong but US, UK eye rates.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS-Currencies strong but US, UK eye rates.

text.p: A strong currency often supports debt markets but in the short term this may not be the case for the dollar and sterling, analysts said on Wednesday.
So far dollar strength has underpinned U.S. assets but the tone in Treasuries is cautious because it is still early in the rate tightening cycle and the market is vulnerable to strong economic data.
In Britain, sterling has strengthened as the mark falters against the dollar but there is concern that monetary policy is too loose and inflation may get out of control, analysts said.

"Dollar and sterling are strong and are likely to remain so, but there are major short term concerns in both markets." said John McNeill, bond market strategist at I.D.E.A. in London. "The problem in the U.S. is that the market is still in a jumpy phase in this early part of the tightening cycle."

He said after the first tightening on March 25, when the Federal Reserve rates its fund rate to 5.50 percent, the market had started to ask when the next increase would take place and what the net tightening through the entire cycle would be.
Sonja Gibbs, senior bond strategist at Nomura International in London, said the market was pricing in further tightening.
"Another rate hike is already more or less priced into the short end but the long end has yet to come to grips with it," she said.
Gibbs said the hot issue was where the Japanese would place their new fiscal year allocations, with the likelihood being that they would favour Treasuries.
But, she said some Japanese fund spokesmen have said they would prefer the dollar/yen rate to be a bit lower before they dive into Treasuries.

"That sounds contradictory, given that a strong currency is good for bond markets, but it is not entirely so because where do you go from here?" she said. "The dollar is a mixed bag in terms of where people are going to invest."
At 1219 GMT, the dollar was at 126.48/126.58 yen, just off a new 56-month high of 126.92 hit overnight.
McNeill said only after the next U.S. interest rate rise would things improve for Treasuries.
"The storm clouds are going to clear in the U.S. but it is going to take the next tightening to make the market think there is light at the end of the tunnel," he said.
In Britain, McNeill saw pitfalls for gilts until either interest rates were tightened or there was some unexepctedly weak UK economic data.

"There is a suggestion that (monetary) policy is currently too loose, risks are being taken with inflation and we could suffer the dredded British disease of the boom getting out of control," he said. "The idea that the policy is unbalanced at the moment is dangerous and gilts are only going to benefit once that uncertainty is out of way."

Gibbs said sterling's position was more fragile than that of the dollar, from which it gained support. Sterling was quoted at 2.7870/80 to the mark at 1225 GMT, just below a new 4-1/2 year high of 2.7940 set in early trading.

"We have breached the old ERM (Exchange Rate Mechanism) floor and further upside from here is questionable," she said adding that the gilt market was languishing and likely to continue to do so for now.

Michael Derks, cross market fixed income strategist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London, said strong U.S. and British currencies could mean there was less need to buy yields than the economic fundamentals suggested.
"They will get support from a dampening of economic activity in terms of the exchange rate being stronger," he said.
